title: Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters
goal: By the end you can explain why one bad record stops a whole partition of a log when in a queue it only loops, tell transient from permanent failures, build bounded retries and a dead-letter topic whose headers say where each record came from, and keep one account's payments in order while you do it.

warmup.q: A payment record's amount is "12x50", so parsing it fails every time. Your at-least-once consumer from lesson 7 lets the exception escape, and Kubernetes restarts the pod. What happens to the payments behind it in the same partition?
options: They are processed: Kafka skips a record that fails three times
They wait indefinitely: every restart starts at the committed offset, reaches the same record and crashes again
Kafka moves the bad record to a dead-letter topic after `max.poll.interval.ms`
They move to another partition
warmup.why: Kafka has no idea your code failed; the plain consumer has no retry limit and no dead-letter topic. The committed offset stays before the bad record, so every restart replays from there and fails at the same place. Dead-letter topics exist only if your code or framework writes them. The first option is the tempting belief that Kafka gives up on a record for you. A queue broker would at least count the attempts: a RabbitMQ quorum queue gives up on a message after 20 deliveries by default and drops it, or dead-letters it if you set a dead-letter exchange. A Kafka consumer group counts nothing.

sections.h: One record that always fails stops its whole partition
sections.body:
Lesson 1 of this track met the poison message in a queue: a message that crashes every consumer that takes it, is redelivered, and crashes the next one. On a log the same record does more damage. This lesson shows why, and builds what the log leaves you to build yourself.

pay-3 arrives with the amount `12x50`. Somebody's payment form let a letter through. Parsing it throws `NumberFormatException`, and it will throw every time.

Run that through the at-least-once loop from lesson 7. The loop processes the batch, and the exception escapes before the commit. The pod restarts, starts at the group's committed offset, processes pay-0 to pay-2 again, reaches pay-3 and crashes again. It will do this forever. The Try-it below shows three rounds of it.

A partition is a log with one bookmark per group, and the bookmark can only move past a record once the consumer is done with it. So one record that can't be done holds back everything behind it in its partition. If that partition receives 30 payments a second, 108,000 pile up behind pay-3 in an hour. The other partitions keep flowing, which makes it easy to miss: the group's total lag barely moves. A record that fails every time you process it is a **poison pill**.

Compare lesson 1's queue. Its broker keeps a state for every message, so while a bad message is redelivered, the messages behind it go to other consumers. And the broker counts the attempts: since RabbitMQ 4.0, a quorum queue stops after 20 deliveries by default and drops the message, or dead-letters it if a dead-letter exchange is set. A Kafka consumer group keeps one bookmark per partition and counts nothing, so nothing gives up and nothing behind the record gets past. That is head-of-line blocking, the price of the log's per-partition order. Everything the queue broker did for its poison message, a Kafka consumer has to do itself.

It can fail in two places. In your own code, as here: a bad amount, an unknown currency, a `NullPointerException` in a mapper. Or inside `poll`, in the deserializer, when the bytes aren't what the deserializer expects: a producer that switched to Avro, a corrupted record. Then `poll` hands out the good records in front of the bad one, and on the next call throws `RecordDeserializationException`. The exception names the partition and the offset, and in Kafka 4.4 it also carries the record's raw key and value bytes. The consumer's position stays on the bad record, so every later `poll` throws again. The only way past it is `seek(partition, offset + 1)`, and if you seek without saving those bytes somewhere first, the record is gone for good.

Before choosing a fix, ask why it failed, because the answer decides what helps.

A **transient** failure means the record is fine and something around it was briefly wrong: the card issuer timed out, a database lock wait expired, a downstream service answered 503. The same call can succeed a second later, so retrying is right.

A **permanent** failure means the record, or your code, is wrong: `12x50`, a currency your ledger doesn't know, a bug. Retrying gives the same exception every time, so it only wastes time and blocks the partition.

The consumer has to tell them apart, and it can only do that by the exception's type. Make that list explicit: retry the exceptions you know are transient, and treat everything else as permanent.

try.title: Watch a poison pill stop a partition
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`.

Run `PoisonPillDemo` (command below). It writes six amounts to a new topic; the third is `12x50`. Then it tries three times to get through them, each time with a fresh consumer that starts at the committed offset, as a restarted pod would. Here the handler parses the amount.
Predict, then run it again with `-Pargs=deserialize`: now the value deserializer parses the amount, inside `poll`. On the third try it seeks past the bad record.

alt.title: PoisonPillDemo.kt

try.expect:
Without arguments:
```text
try 1: offset 0 applied 1000 cents
try 1: offset 1 applied 2500 cents
try 1: crashed: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"; no commit
try 2: offset 0 applied 1000 cents
try 2: offset 1 applied 2500 cents
try 2: crashed: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"; no commit
try 3: offset 0 applied 1000 cents
try 3: offset 1 applied 2500 cents
try 3: crashed: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"; no commit
committed offset 0 of 6: lag 6
```
Every restart applied offsets 0 and 1 again and died at offset 2, and offsets 3 to 5 were never reached. With `deserialize` (the client also logs an `ERROR ... Value Deserializers with error` line for each failed poll; left out here):
```text
try 1: offset 0 applied 1000 cents
try 1: offset 1 applied 2500 cents
try 1: poll threw RecordDeserializationException at offset 2 (java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"); position stays 2
try 2: poll threw RecordDeserializationException at offset 2 (java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"); position stays 2
try 3: poll threw RecordDeserializationException at offset 2 (java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12x50"); position stays 2
try 3: seek to 3: offset 2 is skipped, and nobody will see it again
try 3: offset 3 applied 4000 cents
try 3: offset 4 applied 990 cents
try 3: offset 5 applied 7000 cents
committed offset 6 of 6: lag 0
```
`poll` handed out offsets 0 and 1 first, then threw, and the position stayed on offset 2 for every later poll. The seek got the partition moving, and lost the payment: lag 0 here means one payment silently skipped.

frames.say: Now a consumer that sorts failures first. pay-2's call to the card issuer times out: a **transient** failure, because the payment is fine and the issuer was slow. The consumer waits 100 ms and tries again, then 200 ms, and the third attempt works. The number of attempts is capped (3 here), so a failure that never clears can't hold the partition forever.

refs.title: Quarkus: Apache Kafka reference guide (failure strategies and dead-letter queue)

sections.h: Long waits belong in retry topics, not in the poll loop
sections.body:
In-place retries handle a hiccup. They can't handle an outage. Say the card issuer is down for 3 minutes. Waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms give up in under a second, and every payment of those 3 minutes lands in the DLT: 5,400 records for a person to replay. Stretch the waits to 30 seconds and up to 6 attempts instead, and one payment holds its partition for 3 minutes while 5,400 others queue behind it, with the poll loop dangerously close to `max.poll.interval.ms`.

The fix is to wait somewhere else. A queue broker can make one message wait while the rest flow past: since RabbitMQ 4.4 a quorum-queue message can carry a delivery time. A log can't, because its bookmark is one number per partition. So Kafka consumers build the wait out of separate topics. **Retry topics** form a staircase of topics with growing delays: `payments.retry-10s`, then `payments.retry-1m`, then `payments.DLT`. When a record still fails after its quick in-place retries, the main consumer writes it to `payments.retry-10s`, commits, and moves on to the next payment at full speed. The record's timestamp says when it was written, so the retry consumer knows it is due 10 seconds later.

A separate consumer group reads each retry topic. When the head of a partition isn't due yet, it doesn't sleep: it calls `pause` on that partition and keeps calling `poll`, which keeps it in the group (lesson 8) and returns nothing for paused partitions. When the record is due, it calls `resume`, seeks back to the record, and processes it. A failure there sends the record one step down the staircase; the last step is the DLT. Every record in one retry topic waits the same 10 seconds, so they come due in the order they were written, and the consumer only ever waits for the record at the head.

Frameworks build this staircase for you. Spring for Apache Kafka has `@RetryableTopic`; Quarkus has the `delayed-retry-topic` failure strategy. It is worth knowing what they do, because the staircase has a cost they can't hide. A record in a retry topic has left its partition, and the payments behind it in that partition carry on without it. For many records that is fine. For a payment it is a problem, and the next section deals with it.

refs.title: KafkaConsumer (Kafka 4.4 javadoc): pause, resume and seek

analogy: Think of a cashier's lane at a supermarket. A customer whose card is declined because the terminal lost its connection can wait a moment and try again: that is a transient failure, and a couple of retries fix it. A customer with a cart full of items that have no price can't be served by trying again. A good cashier doesn't hold the whole queue: the cart goes to the service desk with a note saying what was wrong, and the queue moves on. That desk is the dead-letter topic, and the note is the headers. The analogy breaks with families: if the same family has three carts in the queue and the first went to the desk, the other two must follow it there, or the family's purchases get rung up out of order. Real cashiers don't have to care about that. A payments consumer does.
in_your_world: In Quarkus, the SmallRye connector's `failure-strategy` attribute decides what happens when your `@Incoming` method fails: `fail` (the default) stops the channel, which is the poison pill; `ignore` commits past it and loses the payment; `dead-letter-queue` writes it to `dead-letter-topic-<channel>` with headers such as `dead-letter-reason` and `dead-letter-offset`; `delayed-retry-topic` builds the retry staircase. Use SmallRye Fault Tolerance's `@Retry` on the method for quick in-place retries, but list only transient exceptions in it. None of these park keys, so for the ledger, keep a parked-accounts table in Oracle, checked in the same transaction as the idempotency key from lesson 7, and route a parked account's payments to the DLT yourself. If a payment kicks off a Temporal workflow, Temporal's activity retry policy can take over the transient retries, and the Kafka consumer only has to start the workflow.
mistake: Logging and committing past a failure (`catch (e) { log.error(...) }`), or the framework equivalent of `ignore`. The partition never gets stuck, so it looks healthy, and every failure silently loses a payment: a missing ledger entry that someone finds weeks later during reconciliation, with the record long gone by retention. The opposite mistake is just as common: retrying everything forever, which turns one bad record into a stopped partition. The fix: classify exceptions, retry only the transient ones and only a few times, send everything else to a DLT with headers, commit only after the dead letter is acknowledged, and put an alert on the DLT.

compare.title: Building a dead letter in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.src:
fun deadLetter(failed: ConsumerRecord<String, String>, error: Throwable, dlt: String): ProducerRecord<String, String> {
    val record = ProducerRecord<String, String>(dlt, null, failed.key(), failed.value()) // partition from the key
    failed.headers().forEach { record.headers().add(it) }                              // keep the producer's headers
    record.headers()
        .add("dlt.original.topic", failed.topic().toByteArray())
        .add("dlt.original.partition", failed.partition().toString().toByteArray())
        .add("dlt.original.offset", failed.offset().toString().toByteArray())
        .add("dlt.exception.class", error.javaClass.name.toByteArray())
        .add("dlt.exception.message", (error.message ?: "").toByteArray())
    return record
}

compare.note: Header values are bytes in both languages, so every number becomes a string first. Kotlin's `toByteArray()` uses UTF-8 by default; Java's `getBytes()` without an argument uses the platform charset, so the Java version passes UTF-8 explicitly. Kotlin's `?:` replaces the null check on the message: `Exception()` without a message gives null in both. In both, the partition is `null`, so the producer picks it from the key and an account's dead letters stay together and in order.

worked.title: Give the ledger consumer an error path

steps.say: Write down which exceptions are transient. Everything not on the list is permanent and goes to the DLT on the first failure. A list you can read in one screen beats a clever rule.
steps.alt_code:
fun isTransient(e: Throwable): Boolean =
    e is java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException ||                    // the card issuer was slow
        e is IssuerUnavailableException ||                        // our wrapper for a 503
        e is java.sql.SQLTransientException                       // lock wait timeout, connection reset

steps.say: Retry the transient ones a few times with growing waits, and let everything else out at once. With 3 attempts and 100 ms doubling, a payment that keeps failing costs 300 ms of the batch's time, far inside `max.poll.interval.ms`.

In the loop, check parking first, then handle, then dead-letter. Park the key whenever a record goes to the DLT. Commit after the batch, when every dead letter is acknowledged. This is what the lab's `RetryingConsumer` does, with the parked set in memory.

Close the loop for the people who own the DLT. Alert when its end offset grows. Give them a replay tool that reads a parked account's dead letters in order, lets them fix the value, sends each back to `payments` with the same key, and clears the parked entry. The replayed payments carry their original idempotency keys, so a replay that runs twice applies nothing twice.

lab.title: Build a consumer that retries, dead-letters and parks
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 11 fail. `DeadLettersTest` needs nothing; `RetryingConsumerTest` uses `MockConsumer` and `MockProducer`, and passes a `sleep` that only records the waits, so no test really sleeps; `DltOnBrokerTest` runs against a Kafka 4.4 broker.
In `DeadLetters.java`, write `topicFor` and `deadLetter`: same key and value, no partition, the original headers, then the five `dlt.*` headers as UTF-8 strings.

In `RetryingConsumer.kt`, write `pollOnce`. For each record: if its key is parked, dead-letter it with a `ParkedKeyException`; otherwise call the handler, retrying only `TransientFailure` up to `maxAttempts` calls with `sleep(backoff(n))` between them; if it still fails, dead-letter it and park its key as `topic-partition@offset`. Wait for each dead letter's ack. Commit the batch at the end.

Run everything until all 11 pass. The broker test writes 30 payments and a poison pill to 3 partitions, runs your consumer in a real group, reads the dead letter back from the broker with its headers, and checks that the group's lag is 0.
hints: `DeadLetters.header(headers, name)` is given; the tests use it to read your headers back.
Catch `TransientFailure` before `Exception`. A `try` inside a `for (n in 1..maxAttempts)` loop that returns on success keeps the retry logic short.
`MockProducer.history()` is every record your code sent. The test for a failed DLT write sets `sendException`, so `send` throws: let it escape before the commit.

drill.title: The error path from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, the body of a poll loop that retries a `TransientFailure` up to 3 times with waits of 100 and 200 ms, sends anything else (and anything still failing) to `payments.DLT` with its original offset in a header, waits for the broker's ack, and commits after the batch. Then answer: why must the send to the DLT finish before the commit?

recap: A record that fails every time (a poison pill) stops its partition: the bookmark can't pass it and nothing counts the attempts. A queue broker counts deliveries and gives up; a Kafka consumer must do that itself.
Sort failures by exception type: retry transient ones a few times with exponential backoff; send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once.
A dead letter keeps the key and value and adds headers: original topic, partition, offset, exception. Wait for its ack, then commit.
A deserialization failure throws `RecordDeserializationException` from `poll` on every call; seek past it, after saving its bytes.
Long waits go to retry topics with fixed delays, so the main partition keeps moving. Anything that leaves the partition can be overtaken.
For payments, park the key: later records of a failed account follow it to the DLT, in order, until it is resolved.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: to go faster, a consumer sends dead letters with `send()` and doesn't wait for the result, then commits. The DLT's partition leader is down for a minute, and the pod crashes during that minute. What happens to a poison pill it dead-lettered just before the crash?
options: It is in the DLT: `send()` returned without an error
It is processed again after the restart
It may be lost: the commit moved past it while its dead letter was still unsent, and the crash dropped the dead letter
The producer's idempotence keeps it safe
quiz.why: `send()` only puts the record in the producer's buffer (lesson 6). The commit is what makes the consumer never read it again. If the buffered dead letter dies with the process after the commit, the record is in neither place. Waiting for `send(...).get()` before the commit keeps the at-least-once order from lesson 7. Idempotence prevents duplicates from retries; it doesn't save unsent records.

quiz.q: The same poison message reaches a RabbitMQ 4.x quorum queue read by two competing consumers, with no dead-letter exchange, and a Kafka consumer group running the plain at-least-once loop. With default settings, what happens in each?
options: The queue redelivers it until its delivery count passes 20, then drops it, while other messages keep flowing; the Kafka partition stops behind it until your code does something
Both stop: no broker ever skips a message
Both move it to a dead-letter destination after 5 attempts
Kafka skips it after `max.poll.interval.ms`; the queue redelivers it forever
quiz.why: The quorum queue keeps a delivery count per message and, since RabbitMQ 4.0, gives up after 20 by default. Without a dead-letter exchange it drops the message, which is a silent loss of its own. Meanwhile the other messages go to the other consumer. The consumer group has one bookmark per partition and no count, so the record blocks its partition until your code retries, dead-letters or skips it. `max.poll.interval.ms` only throws a slow member out, and five attempts is the default of Kafka's share groups, which lesson 11 covers.

quiz.q: A partition has been stuck on one record for 20 minutes; the handler throws `IllegalArgumentException` every time. A colleague suggests raising `max.poll.interval.ms` to 30 minutes. What does that change?
options: It fixes it: the consumer gets more time to process the record
Nothing useful: the record fails the same way however long you wait; it needs to go to a DLT
It moves the record to another consumer
It makes Kafka skip the record
quiz.why: `max.poll.interval.ms` only decides when a slow loop is thrown out of the group (lesson 8). A deterministic failure isn't slow, it is wrong, and more time changes nothing. The record has to leave the partition: a dead-letter topic, with headers so it can be fixed and replayed.

quiz.q: Your consumer catches `RecordDeserializationException` from `poll`, logs it, and calls `poll` again. What happens?
options: The next poll returns the records after the bad one
The broker deletes the bad record
The consumer switches to `read_uncommitted`
The next poll throws the same exception again, because the position is still on the bad record
quiz.why: The consumer's position doesn't move past a record it couldn't deserialize. Every `poll` reaches it again and throws again. Save the raw bytes from the exception (`keyBuffer()` and `valueBuffer()`) to a DLT, then `seek(e.topicPartition(), e.offset() + 1)`.

quiz.q: acct-7's capture went to the DLT, and the consumer parks acct-7 in an in-memory set. Then a deploy restarts the pod. acct-7's next payment, a refund, arrives. What happens?
options: It is parked, because the DLT remembers acct-7
It is applied: the new process starts with an empty parked set, so the refund overtakes the failed capture
It is rejected by the broker
The consumer replays the DLT on start-up
quiz.why: Nothing reads the DLT back automatically, so after a restart (or a rebalance that moves the partition) an in-memory set is empty. Keep parked keys where they survive, a database table or a compacted topic keyed by account, and load them when the partition is assigned.

flashcards.back: A record that fails every time it is processed. Without special handling it stops its partition: the committed offset can never pass it.

flashcards.front: Transient or permanent: how do you decide, and what do you do with each?
flashcards.back: By exception type. Transient (timeouts, 503s, lock waits): retry a few times with backoff. Permanent (bad data, bugs): dead-letter at once.

flashcards.front: Which headers should a dead letter carry?
flashcards.back: The original topic, partition and offset, and the exception's class and message. Keep the producer's own headers too.

flashcards.front: In which order do you write the dead letter and commit?
flashcards.back: Send the dead letter and wait for the ack, then commit. A failed DLT write must leave the record uncommitted.
It throws again on every call: the position stays on the bad record until you `seek` to offset + 1.
A DLT or retry topic takes a record out of its partition, so later records of the same key would overtake it. Parking sends them after it.

terms.plain: A record that fails every time it is processed, so it blocks its partition.
A failure caused by something briefly wrong around the record, such as a timeout; a retry can succeed.
A failure caused by the record or the code; the same input fails the same way every time.
Waiting longer before each retry, for example 100, 200, then 400 ms.
A topic where a consumer puts records it gave up on, with headers saying where they came from and why.
A named byte value attached to a Kafka record next to its key and value.
A topic that holds failed records for a fixed delay before another consumer tries them again.
Sending all later records of a failed key after it, so the key's records stay in order.

explain_back.prompt: On-call got paged: one partition of `payments` has a lag of 40,000 and growing, while the other eleven are at 0. Explain what most likely happened, why the other partitions are fine, and what the consumer should do differently.
explain_back.answer: Most likely a poison pill: one record in that partition fails every time we process it, say an amount we can't parse. Our consumer lets the exception escape before the commit, so it restarts at the committed offset, reaches the same record and fails again, forever. The bookmark can't move past it, so every payment written to that partition since then is waiting. The other partitions have their own bookmarks and other members' attention, so they keep flowing. The consumer should sort failures: retry the transient ones, like issuer timeouts, a few times with backoff; send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once, with headers for the original topic, partition, offset and exception; wait for that write's ack and then commit. Because these are payments, it should also park the account, so the account's later payments go to the DLT behind the failed one instead of overtaking it, and keep the parked accounts in a table so a restart doesn't forget them. Then someone fixes the record and replays the account's dead letters in order, and the idempotency keys make the replay safe.

deeper.body:
**Saving undeserializable records.** When `poll` throws `RecordDeserializationException`, the exception holds everything you need to dead-letter the record without the deserializer: `topicPartition()`, `offset()`, `timestamp()`, `headers()`, and the raw `keyBuffer()` and `valueBuffer()`. Write those bytes to the DLT with a byte-array producer, then `seek` past. Another approach is to consume as `byte[]` and deserialize in your handler, so a bad record becomes an ordinary handler failure. Spring's `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` wraps a deserializer to do the same.

**Retry topics without sleeping.** The retry consumer's trick is `pause(partitions)` plus `poll`. A paused partition returns no records, but the loop keeps calling `poll`, so the member stays in the group and `max.poll.interval.ms` is never in danger. Store the due time in a header or compute it from the record timestamp, and `resume` the partition when the head record is due. Use one topic per delay: if a topic mixed 10-second and 10-minute delays, a 10-minute record at the head would hold back 10-second records behind it.

**Share groups and acknowledgements.** Lesson 11 covers share groups, where each record is acknowledged on its own: `RELEASE` returns it for another attempt, `REJECT` gives up on it, and the broker counts deliveries (`share.delivery.count.limit`, 5 by default). Kafka 4.4 added a broker-side dead-letter queue for share groups (KIP-1191). They give up per-key order across consumers, so for payments the parking problem above remains yours.
